source.title: The Diminishing Returns of Masked Language Models to Science
source.authors: Zhi Hong; A. Ajith; J. Pauloski; Eamon Duede; K. Chard; I. Foster

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task performance across model sizes, pretraining data sizes, and pretraining durations in scientific masked language models. This is a different measure and setting from the held-out cross-entropy scaling measurements in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss curves that decrease with training iterations, but does not test held-out loss power laws, fit exponents, extrapolate loss from smaller runs, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It cites scaling-law work as related research; cited results are not recorded as findings here. Detailed per-model task scores appear in Tables 2, 3, 6, and 7; rows below record the paper's explicit aggregate comparisons and conclusions.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains its own masked LMs (340M and 770M parameters, 2.2B to 221B tokens, 0.9k to 33k iterations) and reports downstream F1 on 12 scientific tasks as model size, data and pretraining length vary. This bears on V6 (downstream gains with scale) in a new setting: encoder-only MLMs on science information extraction. It fits no power law, extrapolates nothing and measures no held-out loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that model size, pretraining data, pretraining time and finetuning time do not significantly or consistently improve scientific information-extraction performance, with gains highly task-dependent. They attribute this to the power of finetuning, limited evaluation datasets, and ScholarBERT models being small relative to their corpus. They also find domain-specific pretraining does not guarantee gains, except for biomedicine.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates masked language models on downstream scientific-task F1, rather than fitting held-out cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported model-size effect differs by downstream task type: relation extraction improves consistently, while NER and sentence classification do not. Data-size comparisons also vary across tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: ScholarBERT training loss drops rapidly only in the first ~10k iterations, then flattens (Fig. 1). This is single-run training loss, not held-out loss, and no fit is made.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLM pretraining on a 221B-token science corpus saturates 340M–770M models early in a single pass.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The authors note that their 12 labeled test datasets cover only five domains plus two multidisciplinary datasets, with five datasets from biomedicine, and that the largest model (770M parameters) may be too small to demonstrate language-model scaling laws. The reported F1 scores are averaged over five runs; extended tables report standard deviations.
record.rows_left_out: The individual model-by-task F1 results in Tables 2, 3, 6, and 7 are not separately transcribed here; the rows capture the paper's explicit aggregate comparisons and task-type findings. The paper reports the full score matrices in those tables.

untested.parts: No held-out loss is measured and no power-law fit is made. Only training-loss curves are shown (Fig. 1).
Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data, or transfer power-law fit.
No predictive fit of downstream score to scale or loss. Model size spans only ~110M–770M. Downstream score is not related to pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: Per-model mean F1 (NER and RE/SC) for each scaling pair, showing NER-mean declines for SB_100→XL_100 (76.46→75.68) and XL_1→XL_100 (76.12→75.68)
Downstream results for intermediate pretraining checkpoints (5k, 10k, 23k). The paper describes them but gives no numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new setting (encoder MLMs, scientific downstream tasks) rather than a different method for the originals' loss question. The scale range is narrow (~7x in parameters), so it cannot test predictability over orders of magnitude. The paper's 10/12 count for SB-XL_1 vs SB-XL_100 conflicts with its own Table 2–3 values. Several Battery scores have large SDs (up to ±5.8), making individual comparisons noisy.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fits and the non-bottleneck conditions.
No small-run loss fits or large-run loss predictions are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
The study does not isolate depth, width, or architecture effects at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns scientific text pretraining and downstream tasks, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer power-law forms.

It compares downstream F1 across selected model sizes, data sizes, and training checkpoints, but does not fit a predictive relationship to held-out pretraining loss or evaluate downstream predictability over several orders of magnitude.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across choices of parameter counting, schedule, data, or fitting method.

rows.subject: BERT-Base and BERT-Large
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream F1 at two model sizes with the same training data.
rows.measure: Downstream task F1; number of tasks where scores were within 1 percentage point
rows.baseline: BERT-Base; exact paired task scores are in Tables 2 and 3
rows.value: BERT-Large; within 1 percentage point on 6/12 tasks
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate comparison
rows.note: The authors state that a larger model did not always produce a significant improvement; this aggregate comparison covers the 12-task evaluation.
rows.check: Count checks against Tables 2–3 (6/12 within 1pp). Both means rose (NER 74.75→76.44; RE/SC 81.95→84.56). Note the BERT pair is ~110M→340M, a 3x step, not orders of magnitude.

rows.subject: ScholarBERT_1 and ScholarBERT-XL_1
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream F1 at two model sizes with the same pretraining data subset.
rows.measure: Downstream task F1; number of tasks where scores were within 1 percentage point
rows.baseline: ScholarBERT_1; exact paired task scores are in Tables 2 and 3
rows.value: ScholarBERT-XL_1; within 1 percentage point on 7/12 tasks
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate comparison
rows.note: The authors report that the larger model did not always yield a significant gain.
rows.check: Means barely move (NER 76.08→76.12; RE/SC 80.87→81.86). The XL model is worse on Battery (94.67→88.75), and that score has a high SD (±4.0).

rows.value: ScholarBERT-XL_100; within 1 percentage point on 6/12 tasks

rows.check: The NER mean falls with the larger model (76.46→75.68). NCBI, SciERC-NER and ScienceExam drop >1pp. RE/SC mean rises (82.33→84.82). The row should note these declines.

rows.subject: ScholarBERT-XL_1 and ScholarBERT-XL_100
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream F1 across pretraining data sizes at the same model size.
rows.measure: Downstream task F1; number of tasks where scores were within 1 percentage point
rows.baseline: ScholarBERT-XL_1 trained on PRD_1; exact paired task scores are in Tables 2 and 3
rows.value: ScholarBERT-XL_100 trained on PRD_100; within 1 percentage point on 10/12 tasks
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate comparison
rows.note: The authors say more pretraining data did not guarantee significant downstream gains.
rows.check: The paper's '10/12 within 1pp' does not reproduce from Tables 2–3. By the table, about 6/12 are within 1pp. SciERC-RE (+6.1) and Battery (+6.7) rise >1pp. SciERC-NER, MatSciNER, Coleridge and ChemProt fall >1pp. The NER mean drops 76.12→75.68. The row should flag this discrepancy and the declines.

rows.subject: BERT-Base, BERT-Large, ScholarBERT_1, ScholarBERT-XL_1, ScholarBERT_100, and ScholarBERT-XL_100
rows.operation_detail: Compared smaller and larger models with the same training data.

conditions.value: BERT-Base to BERT-Large; ScholarBERT_1 to ScholarBERT-XL_1; ScholarBERT_100 to ScholarBERT-XL_100

rows.baseline: Smaller model in each pair; exact task scores are in Table 3
rows.value: The authors state that relation extraction tasks consistently gained more than 1 percentage point F1 when moving from smaller to larger models.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate statement
rows.note: This is the task-specific condition the authors identify as showing consistent improvements with model size.
rows.check: Verified in Table 3. SciERC-RE: +5.2, +1.8, +4.8. ChemProt: +4.4, +7.6, +1.6 for the three pairs.

rows.subject: BERT-Base, BERT-Large, ScholarBERT_1, ScholarBERT-XL_1, ScholarBERT_100, and ScholarBERT-XL_100
rows.operation_detail: Compared smaller and larger models with the same training data.

conditions.value: BERT-Base to BERT-Large; ScholarBERT_1 to ScholarBERT-XL_1; ScholarBERT_100 to ScholarBERT-XL_100

rows.baseline: Smaller model in each pair; exact task scores are in Tables 2 and 3
rows.value: The authors state that NER and sentence classification did not show consistent significant improvements with larger models.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate statement
rows.note: The paper distinguishes these task types from relation extraction, which showed consistent gains.
rows.check: Aggregate text claim. Tables show some NER tasks falling with size, e.g. ScienceExam 83.12→80.72 for SB_100→XL_100.

rows.subject: ScholarBERT(-XL) checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance across pretraining checkpoints and finetuning durations.
rows.baseline: 0.9k-iteration checkpoint finetuned for 5 epochs; exact value not stated
rows.value: The 0.9k-iteration model received the largest boost, +8%, in downstream F1 with 75 rather than 5 finetuning epochs.
rows.note: The reported change includes more finetuning as well as an undertrained checkpoint; it is not an isolated pretraining-scale effect.
rows.check: The effect is of finetuning epochs (5 vs 75) at a fixed pretraining checkpoint. This is not a scale-of-pretraining effect, so it bears on no version.

rows.subject: ScholarBERT(-XL) checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance of a short-pretrained checkpoint with a longer-pretrained checkpoint.

conditions.value: 0.9k iterations with 75 finetuning epochs versus 33k iterations with 5 finetuning epochs

rows.baseline: 33k-iteration model with 5 finetuning epochs; exact value not stated
rows.value: The 0.9k-iteration model with 75 finetuning epochs was 19.9 percentage points lower.
rows.note: The comparison changes both pretraining checkpoint and finetuning duration.
rows.check: Longer pretraining (33k vs 0.9k iterations) gives 19.9pp higher average F1, even though the longer-pretrained model had less finetuning (5 vs 75 epochs). The confound biases against the effect, so the state should be observed, not partial. Intermediate checkpoints (5k, 10k, 23k) are not reported numerically.

rows.subject: ScholarBERT(-XL) checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance after two finetuning durations at the 33k-iteration checkpoint.
rows.baseline: 5 finetuning epochs; exact value not stated
rows.value: 75 finetuning epochs produced an average F1 score only 0.39 percentage points higher.
rows.note: This is a finetuning-duration comparison, not a parameter/token/compute scaling test.
rows.check: Finetuning-duration comparison only (+0.39pp). Not pretraining scale.

relationships.condition: Relation extraction tasks across model-size pairs; longer vs very short pretraining
relationships.reason: RE F1 rises >1pp in all three size pairs (R7). The 33k-iteration model beats the 0.9k-iteration model by 19.9pp average F1 (R10).
relationships.display_finding: F1 increased by more than 1 percentage point in all three model-size pairs, and 33k pretraining iterations outperformed 0.9k iterations by 19.9 percentage points in average F1.

relationships.condition: NER and sentence-classification tasks, model size 110M→340M→770M at fixed data
relationships.reason: Half or more of tasks change <1pp (R1–R3). The NER mean falls for SB_100→XL_100, and the authors report no consistent NER/SC gains (R8).
relationships.display_finding: At least half the tasks changed by less than one percentage point, and mean NER performance declined from SB_100 to XL_100.

relationships.condition: 100x pretraining-data increase at fixed 340M/770M model size
relationships.reason: Most tasks change little (R4–R6). For the 770M model, the NER mean drops and four tasks fall >1pp (R6). The authors suggest the model is too small for the corpus.
relationships.display_finding: Most tasks changed little after a 100-fold data increase, while the 770M model's mean NER score declined and four tasks lost over one percentage point.
